title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: antecedent will to save does not coerce — free-moving means
pass_a_gloss: Now to the matter. I deny that, the antecedent will of God concerning giving eternal salvation to Peter having been posited, his free choice concerning the obtaining of salvation is taken away or hindered: and yet at the same time I assert that, this hypothesis having been posited, he cannot fall from salvation, and consequently, the Divine decree cannot be made void. As to the former; The efficacious will of God not only works all things which God wills, but in that manner, and through those means which he wills. From an efficacious and antecedent purpose therefore of saving Peter, God is not bound to use coercive means, or means necessitating the human will, but it suffices that he use those which the Divine wisdom knows can efficaciously, infallibly, and yet freely move and bend his will. Nay I also add this: While God from the antecedent decree of giving salvation moves the free choice of the elect toward acquiring salvation, so far is it from being lost thence, that rather the liberty of the human will is increased and strengthened. For as Báñez excellently, On 1. q. 22 art. 4, The free choice of the creature receives a participated liberty from the Divine free choice, moving it strongly and sweetly according to the mode of its nature.
pass_b_english: Now to the point. I deny that God's antecedent will to give Peter eternal salvation takes away or hinders his free choice about obtaining it — and yet I affirm that, on that hypothesis, he cannot fall from salvation, so the divine decree cannot be made void. First: God's efficacious will works all he wills, but in the manner and by the means he wills. From an efficacious, antecedent purpose to save Peter he need not use coercive means that necessitate the human will; it is enough to use those Divine wisdom knows can move and bend the will efficaciously, infallibly, yet freely. Indeed, when from the antecedent decree to give salvation God moves the elect's free choice toward acquiring it, liberty is not lost but rather increased and strengthened. As Báñez puts it (In 1. q.22 a.4): the creature's free choice receives participated liberty from Divine free choice, moving it strongly and sweetly according to its nature.
source_text: Jam ad rem. Nego posita antecedente Dei voluntate de danda Petro aeterna salute, tolli aut impediri liberum ejus arbitrium circa salutis consecutionem: et tamen illud simul assero, non posse illum, posita hac hypothesi, a salute excidere, ac per consequens, Divinum decretum non posse fieri irritum. Quod ad prius; Efficax Dei voluntas non modo operatur omnia quae vult Deus, sed eo modo, et per illa media quae vult. Ex efficaci igitur et antecedente proposito salvandi Petrum, non tenetur Deus uti mediis coactivis, aut necessitantibus voluntatem humanam, sed sufficit ut utatur illis, quae sapientia Divina novit efficaciter, infallibiliter, et tamen libere posse movere, et flectere ejus voluntatem. Imo et hoc etiam addo, Dum Deus ex antecedente decreto dandae salutis movet liberum arbitrium electorum ad salutem acquirendam, tantum abest ut inde amittatur, ut potius augeatur et roboretur humanae voluntatis libertas. Nam ut optime Bannes, In 1. qu. 22. art. 4, Liberum creaturae arbitrium accipit libertatem participatam ex Divino libero arbitrio, movente illud fortiter et suaviter juxta modum suae naturae.
